cards.title: Addressing Japanese Seniors
cards.body: Japanese culture values hierarchy. Use formal titles and last names for seniors. Hand gestures and bowing show respect. Learn basic Japanese phrases for greetings and addressing superiors.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints in Japan
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Carry identification at all times. Be polite and patient. Security staff may not speak English. Use simple Japanese phrases or gestures to communicate.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Japan
cards.body: In Japan, hierarchy is important. Use formal titles (e.g., -san) and last names when addressing seniors. Bow slightly when greeting. Wait for seniors to initiate conversation or actions.
doThis: Address seniors with formal titles and last names
Wait for seniors to initiate conversation or actions
avoidThis: Use first names or informal language with seniors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Saving Face in Japan
cards.body: Criticism should be given privately and tactfully. Disagree politely and indirectly. Refuse requests gently to avoid causing offense.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Refusal
cards.body: In Japan, hierarchy is crucial. When refusing, address seniors with respect. Use indirect language to avoid direct disagreement. This maintains harmony and respect.
doThis: Address seniors by their family name and appropriate title
avoidThis: Disagree openly without consideration for hierarchy

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Saving Face in Refusal
cards.body: Japanese prioritize saving face. When refusing, avoid direct 'no'. Use ambiguous language like 'maybe' or 'it's difficult'. This helps maintain relationships and respect.
doThis: Use ambiguous language instead of direct 'no'
avoidThis: Make the other person feel embarrassed

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Japan
cards.body: Japanese culture values hierarchy and respect. Address seniors with their family name followed by their rank or title. Avoid using first names unless invited to do so. Use honorific language to show respect.
doThis: Wait for seniors to initiate bowing or handshakes

cards.title: Saving Face in Japan
cards.body: Japanese people value harmony and avoiding embarrassment. Be indirect when criticizing or disagreeing. Use polite language and avoid public confrontation. If you must refuse, do so gently and politely.

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints in Japan
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Carry ID at all times. Follow instructions calmly. Be patient with security staff and local nationals. Avoid rushing or showing frustration.
doThis: Be patient with security staff and local nationals

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Japan
cards.body: Japanese culture values hierarchy and respect for seniors. Use formal titles and last names when addressing superiors. Avoid direct disagreement to maintain harmony. Women often hold supportive roles in the workplace.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names with superiors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Navigate Gender Roles Carefully
cards.body: Traditional gender roles persist in Japan. Women primarily handle domestic duties. Men are expected to be dedicated to work. Women in the workforce often face challenges due to long hours and lack of childcare. Be mindful of these dynamics when interacting with local civilians.
doThis: Be aware of workplace challenges for women
avoidThis: Assume equal participation in domestic duties

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Japan
cards.body: Japanese culture values respect for elders and leaders, influenced by Shinto and Confucianism. Address seniors with formal titles and use polite language. Avoid public criticism or disagreement with superiors.
doThis: Use formal titles (e.g., '-san', '-sensei') when addressing seniors
Speak politely and respectfully to superiors
Avoid interrupting or contradicting seniors in public
avoidThis: Using first names or informal language with superiors
Publicly criticizing or disagreeing with seniors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Saving Face in Japan
cards.body: To save face, avoid direct confrontation or public criticism. Use indirect language and show empathy. Refusal is often implied rather than stated outright.
doThis: Use indirect language when disagreeing or refusing
Show empathy and understanding in conversations
avoidThis: Losing your temper or showing strong emotions

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Gift Giving: Hierarchy and Respect
cards.body: Gifts are common in Japan and show respect. Use both hands when giving or receiving gifts. Present gifts neatly wrapped with a bow. Avoid giving gifts in sets of four, as it's considered unlucky. Present gifts to seniors first, showing deference to hierarchy.
doThis: Use both hands when giving/receiving gifts
avoidThis: Give gifts in sets of four

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Gift Giving: Saving Face
cards.body: Save face by avoiding public criticism or disagreement. If you must refuse, do so politely and privately. Use indirect language to soften refusals. Gifts can help maintain harmony and show appreciation.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy at Meals
cards.body: Japanese culture values hierarchy. Show respect to seniors by letting them start eating first. Use proper titles like '-san' or '-sama' when addressing them.
doThis: Wait for seniors to start eating

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Drink Refill Etiquette
cards.body: In Japan, it's polite to refill others' drinks, not your own. Finish your drink to signal you want more. Toast (kanpai) before drinking in social settings.
avoidThis: Drink without toasting in social settings

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Meetings
cards.body: Japanese culture values hierarchy. Address seniors with their rank and last name. Wait for them to initiate a less formal approach. Avoid direct disagreement; instead, express concerns carefully.
doThis: Address seniors with their rank and last name.
Wait for seniors to initiate less formal interaction.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints and Security
cards.body: At checkpoints, present identification promptly. Be polite and patient with security staff. Avoid discussing sensitive topics in public areas.
doThis: Be polite and patient with security staff.
avoidThis: Discuss sensitive topics in public areas.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Addressing Seniors on Radio
cards.body: In Japan's air force, rank is important. Use last names with appropriate honorifics like '-san' for peers or '-sama' for superiors. Avoid first names unless invited. On radio, clearly state your rank and name first.
doThis: State your rank and name first on radio

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Japan (2025)

cards.title: Radio Etiquette in Japan
cards.body: Japanese prefer indirect communication to save face. Be polite and avoid blunt criticism or disagreement on radio. If you must refuse, use phrases like 'it's difficult' instead of a direct 'no'.
